procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 21, 1967 of the Patna High Court in Criminal Revision No. 546 of 1965.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Sub-Divisional Magistrate upheld a preliminary objection based on the absence of previous sanction under s. 197, Cr. P.C. The Second Additional Sessions Judge, on revision, agreed with this view. On further revision, the Patna High Court disagreed with the view taken by the two courts below and holding s. 197, Cr. P.C. to be inapplicable to the case directed the Sub-Divisional Magistrate to make further enquiry into the petition of complaint.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, Bhagwan Prasad Srivastava, assailed the view taken by the High Court. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complainant's case is covered by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making previous sanction from a superior authority necessary before the trial court can take cognizance of the complaint.

facts: The appellant, a civil surgeon, was accused in a complaint of using defamatory and abusive words against the complainant.
The appellant was also accused of having the complainant pushed out of the hospital's operation theatre by the hospital cook.
law: Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code protects public servants from frivolous or false prosecutions for offenses alleged to have been committed while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.

This protection does not cover every offense committed by a public servant, but only those acts that are "directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have been done by virtue of the office."
Whether a particular act is done in the discharge of official duty is a question of fact to be determined by the circumstances of each case.
application: The Court examined the specific acts alleged against the civil surgeon: using defamatory words and having the complainant forcibly removed by a cook.
It found that there was nothing on the record to show that these actions were a part of the appellant's official duty as a Civil Surgeon.
The Court concluded that the alleged acts were not so directly connected with the performance of his official duty that he could not have properly discharged his duty without performing them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the case was not covered by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Therefore, previous sanction from a superior authority was not necessary for the trial court to take cognizance of the complaint.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the complainant's case is covered by Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, making previous sanction from a superior authority necessary before the trial court can take cognizance of the complaint.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, a Civil Surgeon, argued that the alleged acts (using defamatory and abusive words and having the complainant removed from the operation theatre) were interrelated with his official duty and were done in the discharge of that duty. Therefore, he was entitled to the protection of Section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code, which requires prior sanction from a superior authority before a court can take cognizance of the complaint.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the alleged acts of using defamatory and abusive words and having him forcibly removed by a cook were not part of the appellant's official duty as a Civil Surgeon, nor were they so directly connected with the performance of his official duty that he could not have discharged his duty without performing those acts. Therefore, Section 197 was inapplicable, and no prior sanction was necessary.

cases.principle: The question of whether a particular act is done by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially one of fact to be determined on the circumstances of each case.

cases.principle: The question of whether a particular act is done by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially one of fact to be determined on the circumstances of each case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The determination of whether a public servant's act requires sanction for prosecution is a question of fact dependent on the circumstances of each case, hinging on whether the alleged act was so directly connected with the performance of official duty that the duty could not have been properly discharged without it.
obiter: The protection afforded to public servants should neither be construed so narrowly that it becomes ineffective, as it is never an official duty to commit an offence, nor so widely as to violate the principle of legal equality.
The focus of examination is not the 'duty' itself, but the 'act' and its connection to that duty.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the present case the alleged offence consists of the use of defamatory and abusive words and of getting the complainant forcibly turned out of the operation theatre by the Cook. There is nothing on the record to show that this was a part of the official duty of the appellant as Civil Surgeon or that it was so directly connected with the performance of his official duty that without so acting he could not have properly discharged it.
legal_tests_applied: The question whether a particular act is done by a public servant in the discharge of his official duty is substantially one of fact to be determined on the circumstances of each case.
It is not the "duty" which requires examination so much as the "act" because the official act can be performed both in the discharge of the official duty as well as in dereliction of it.

There must be a reasonable connection between the act and the discharge of official duty; the act must bear such relation to the duty that the accused could lay a reasonable claim, but not a pretended or fanciful claim, that he did it in the course of the performance of his duty.

It is the quality of the act that is important and if it falls within the scope and range of the official duties of the public servant concerned the protection contemplated by s. 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code will be attracted.
why_appellant_lost: We do not find any material on the existing record suggesting that the impugned acts were done by the appellant in the discharge of his official duty or that they are directly connected with it.

There was nothing on the record to show that this was a part of the official duty of the appellant as Civil Surgeon or that it was so directly connected with the performance of his official duty that without so acting he could not have properly discharged it.
why_respondent_won: The alleged offence consists of the use of defamatory and abusive words and of getting the complainant-respondent forcibly turned out of the operation theatre, by the Cook. There was nothing on the record to show that this was a part of the official duty of the appellant as Civil Surgeon.
policy_considerations: The object and purpose underlying section 197 Cr. P.C. is to afford protection to public servants against frivolous, vexatious or false prosecution for offences alleged to have been committed by them while acting or purporting to act in the discharge of their official duty.

The larger interest of efficiency of State administration demands that public servants should be free to perform their official duty fearlessly and undeterred by apprehension of their possible prosecution at the instance of private parties to whom annoyance or injury may have been caused by their legitimate acts done in the discharge of their official duty.
It is neither to be too narrowly construed nor too widely. Too narrow and pedantic construction may render it otiose for it is no part of an official duty-and never can be-to commit an offence.

One must also guard against too wide a construction because in our constitutional set up the idea of legal equality or of universal subjection of all citizens to one law administered by the ordinary courts has been pushed to its utmost limits by enshrining equality before the law in our fundamental principles.
